title: No countable list of hosts contains all the stated avoiding populations

plain_language.question: Could a countable catalogue of host populations contain every population that avoids a fixed infinite label pattern?
plain_language.what_we_learned: No. From any such avoiding population, one can construct another that escapes every host on the list, even with exactly one parent of each label and any finite global allowance for stretching edges.
plain_language.what_it_lets_someone_do: Rule out a precise universal-catalogue proposal while retaining the original population conditions, actual roots and fixed-pattern avoidance.
plain_language.what_cannot_conclude: This construction does not preserve a fixed bound on children, forbid terminal individuals or exclude noninjective or arbitrarily stretched maps.

exact_statement_and_scope: Fix an actual Alexander population P avoiding an infinite label word s. For every countable family of actual population hosts U_j, there is one positive finite-fibre terminal clone Q of a one-parent-per-label selection of P such that Q avoids s, its actual roots are canonically equivalent to P's, and every nonroot has exactly one incoming parent of every label. Every infinite word realized by Q is realized by P. For every j, every finite global stretch L and every injective map Q→U_j, some source edge does not map to an undirected host path of length at most L. Hosts need not avoid s or have exact parent counts. The actual population assumptions are infinitude, real chronological birthdates with finite birth sublevels, finitely many roots and children per vertex, functional edge labels and parent coverage at each nonroot. Parent selection can shrink the original language; terminal cloning preserves the selected language exactly. For an already exact-parent P, cloning preserves the whole original language. There is no uniform child cap, no terminal-free condition and no uncountable-host or unbounded-stretch conclusion.

origin.detail: Alexander's 2013 Biologically unavoidable sequences, §6, explicitly asks about universal avoiding populations. This is a negative answer under the specified injective, finite-global-stretch convention, not every possible interpretation of the open-ended question.
